visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not

claims.claim: The query's 1-phenyl-3-methylpyrazolone core is structurally analogous to the 1-phenyl-3-methylpyrazole DPP-4 inhibitor in this context, which is reported to have 75–87% oral bioavailability in humans and no significant food influence.
Pirfenidone, a 1-phenyl-5-methylpyridin-2-one, is rapidly absorbed with high oral bioavailability, supporting the same phenyl-methyl-lactam motif as the query.
Urapidil, an N-methylated pyrimidinedione with a phenylpiperazine substituent, has absolute oral bioavailability of 72–78% in humans.
Alogliptin, an N-methylated uracil DPP-4 inhibitor, has approximately 100% absolute oral bioavailability.
Even under rifampin pretreatment, ondansetron absolute oral bioavailability was 0.40 ± 0.05, still above the 20% threshold.
Other reference molecules in the training contexts also exceed the threshold (duvelisib 42%; ziprasidone 30–60%), so the evidence direction is uniformly supportive of F ≥ 20%.

No query-specific fasted-state or IV-comparator study is provided; fasted inference relies on structural analogs and absence of food-dependent liabilities.
Some records are group-level or unspecified bioavailability type rather than query-matched absolute measurements.
